protocol.legal_basis: No prescribing legal instrument, regulation or poisons schedule provision is printed anywhere in this document.
protocol.supervision_model: Not stated using 'collaborative'/'autonomous' terminology; document states pharmacists are advised to exercise professional discretion and judgement and must prescribe medicines according to the specified sections of the current online version of the Therapeutic Guidelines.
protocol.scope_summary: Queensland Community Pharmacy clinical practice guideline for pharmacist management of impetigo. Service restricted to patients aged 1 year or over. Covers 'Refer when' triggers (with ARF risk and endemic-community criteria referencing Table 1), key points (including case-by-case assessment and possible referral for IM benzathine benzylpenicillin for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander patients), patient history, examination and clinical features (non-bullous, bullous, ecthyma), investigations (skin swab), complications (APSGN, ARF, sepsis), development of a management plan (topical vs oral anti-infective rules, NB1 antimicrobial stewardship), confirmation of management, communication of the plan, general advice, clinical review and follow-up. Ineligibility for treatment as part of a prescribing service does not preclude a patient from accessing services provided as part of usual pharmacy care.

diagnosis_pathways.name: Pharmacist assessment and management of impetigo (history, examination, investigations, referral screening, ARF risk, treatment, confirmation, counselling and review)

steps.description: Patient history: Obtain sufficient information from the patient to assess the safety and appropriateness of any recommendations and medicines. The patient history should consider: age; weight (if a child); pregnancy and lactation status (if applicable); ethnicity (Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander, Māori or Pacific Islander); most recent place of residence/community and/or recent travel to a place where impetigo or ARF may be endemic (a high rate of ARF within the population); onset, duration, nature, location and extent of lesions; recent skin, throat or other infections (e.g. respiratory tract infection) and treatment received; other signs and symptoms e.g., pain, lymphadenopathy, signs of sepsis or other complications (including APSGN and ARF) such as fever, confusion, tachycardia, hypotension or hypertension, clammy skin, vomiting and diarrhoea, facial or peripheral oedema, severe headache, joint pain and/or hot swollen joints, swelling beneath impetigo lesions; potential source of infection e.g., skin trauma, contact with people with similar symptoms; underlying medical conditions including, skin conditions or immunosuppression that may lead to complications (e.g., atopic dermatitis, scabies, herpes simplex); current and recently ceased treatments (including prescribed medicines, vitamins, herbs, other supplements and over-the-counter medicines); drug allergies/adverse reactions; other risk factors including poor hygiene, day care settings, crowding and malnutrition. Reminder: pharmacists can access a range of clinical information in a patient's My Health Record, including details about current and past medication history, allergies and current medical conditions.

gates.criterion: Sufficient information obtained to assess the safety and appropriateness of any recommendations and medicines

No signs of sepsis or other complications (including APSGN and ARF) such as fever, confusion, tachycardia, hypotension or hypertension, clammy skin, vomiting and diarrhoea, facial or peripheral oedema, severe headache, joint pain and/or hot swollen joints, swelling beneath impetigo lesions (RF-26)

steps.description: Examination - Clinical features and presenting symptoms: Impetigo can be classified as primary or secondary form: the primary form is a direct bacterial infection of otherwise healthy skin; the second form (most common) is bacterial infection of a break in the skin from trauma or pruritic conditions (impetiginisation) (6-8). Impetigo may have a similar presentation or co-occur with other common skin conditions including contact dermatitis, thermal burns, folliculitis, dermatophytosis, candidiasis, eczema, scabies, herpes zoster, atopic dermatitis, varicella or molluscum contagiosum (4, 9-10). Table 1. Types of impetigo (1, 2, 7, 11-13): Non-bullous - thin-walled pustules or vesicles that may be itchy, usually not painful, rupture quickly and progress to honey-coloured crusts, minimal or no surrounding erythema; may start with a single vesicle that coalesces with others, often self-inoculation leads to multiple lesions particularly on the face and extremities; patients are generally otherwise well although they may have regional lymphadenopathy; lesions may resolve spontaneously within 2-4 weeks without treatment and heal without scarring. Bullous - irritating, larger (diameter often > 1 cm) fluid-filled vesicles and blisters that rupture quickly to broad-based bullae, and progress to a thin, flat yellow/brown crust; tends to occur on moist intertriginous areas including the nappy area, axillae and neck, as well as the face, trunk and extremities; lesions typically have scaling on the border of the bullae (collarette); patients with bullous impetigo are more likely to experience systemic symptoms including fever, malaise and lymphadenopathy. Ecthyma (deep impetigo) - crusted sores with underlying ulcers; if the crust is removed, an indurated ulcer will appear red, swollen and oozing; most commonly affects the buttocks, thighs, legs, ankles and feet; people more likely to develop ecthyma include children, immunocompromised people, people with untreated impetigo and people living in crowded conditions with poor hygiene; lymphadenopathy may occur; lesions resolve slowly and sometimes spontaneously without treatment, although they may gradually enlarge and also scar.

gates.criterion: Diagnosis is clear and conditions with similar presentation (contact dermatitis, thermal burns, folliculitis, dermatophytosis, candidiasis, eczema, scabies, herpes zoster, atopic dermatitis, varicella, molluscum contagiosum) excluded - see RF-1 'unclear diagnosis'
Impetigo is not classified as widespread, severe and/or ecthyma (ulceration) present (RF-9)

steps.description: Investigations: Non-bullous impetigo infection can be caused by Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A streptococcus), or both. Bullous impetigo is usually caused by Staphylococcus aureus (2, 7). Patients with impetigo do not require an initial skin swab prior to commencing empirical antibiotic therapy unless the diagnosis is uncertain or impetigo is recurrent (2, 7, 12).

gates.criterion: Diagnosis is not uncertain AND impetigo is not recurrent (otherwise skin swab / referral applies - RF-21, RF-1, EXC-14)

steps.description: Screen against the printed 'Refer when' list: Refer the patient to an appropriate healthcare provider (including emergency services, if required) in the following situations: unclear diagnosis; concurrent condition is suspected that cannot be treated in the community pharmacy setting (e.g. viral infection, eczema herpaticum, cellulitis); widespread, painful rash; raised purple rash that doesn’t blanch; generalised erythema that covers ≥90% of skin surface; blistering of skin and mucous membranes (including mouth and eyes); systemic signs or symptoms, including fever, lethargy, headache, rash, nausea and vomiting; chronic sores or ulcers; the impetigo is widespread, severe and/or has ecthyma (ulceration) present; immunocompromised; at high risk of acute rheumatic fever (ARF) (refer to Table 1); patient resides, or has recently resided in an endemic community (refer to Table 1); inadequate response to optimal treatment; infection reoccurs frequently. (See EXC-1 to EXC-14, RF-1 to RF-14.)

gates.criterion: None of the 'Refer when' triggers present (RF-1 to RF-14)

steps.description: ARF risk assessment - Table 1. Individuals at high risk of developing ARF (2, 17, 19): Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people residing in a rural or remote area, or living in a household affected by household overcrowding (>2 people per bedroom) or experiencing socioeconomic disadvantage; Māori and/or Pacific Islander person living in a household affected by overcrowding (>2 people per bedroom) or experiencing socioeconomic disadvantage; a person with a personal history of ARF or RHD; a person with a family or household member with a recent history of ARF or RHD. Additional risk factors for individuals aged ≤40 years (particularly between 5-20 years): people living in a household affected by household overcrowding (>2 people per bedroom) or experiencing socioeconomic disadvantage; people with current or prior residence in (or frequent or recent travel to) an area with a high rate of ARF e.g., refugees and migrants from low-middle income countries, rural and remote communities. People considered at high risk of developing ARF are specified in Table 1. People of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander descent presenting for treatment of impetigo should be assessed on a case-by-case basis to determine the appropriate treatment pathway, and whether referral to an appropriate healthcare provider for treatment with intramuscular (IM) benzathine benzylpenicillin is required (page 2, Key points).

gates.criterion: Patient is not at high risk of developing ARF per Table 1 (RF-11/EXC-11)
Patient does not reside, or has not recently resided in an endemic community, and has no current or prior residence in (or frequent or recent travel to) an area with a high rate of ARF (RF-12/EXC-12)

provenance.section_heading: Table 1. Individuals at high risk of developing ARF

steps.description: Develop management plan: Treatment of impetigo supports skin healing and prevents the development of more serious complications (e.g. sepsis, bone and joint infections, poststreptococcal complications including ARF) (2). Pharmacists must ensure that they are prescribing medicines according to the specified sections of the current online version of the Therapeutic Guidelines. Pharmacist management of impetigo involves: non-pharmacological measures - advice and education to reduce the spread of impetigo as per the Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic (Skin and soft tissue infections - Impetigo) (2) and the Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Impetigo (school sores) fact sheet (20); examination and treatment of co-occurring skin conditions (e.g. dermatitis, scabies, head lice, tinea) or referral to an appropriate healthcare provider; pharmacotherapy (NB1) - a topical or oral medicine mentioned in the Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic (Skin and soft tissue infections - Impetigo) (2). Topical anti-infectives are considered sufficient treatment for patients with nonrecurrent limited non-bullous impetigo (up to 2 sores) who are not at high risk of ARF. Topical antibiotics are not appropriate if the infection is widespread or multiple family/community members are infected, due to the risk of rapid resistance (1-3). Pharmacists may prescribe oral antibiotics if impetigo is in a localised area with more than 2 sores, unless referral criteria apply. See 'Refer when'. NB1: The correct use of antibiotics is essential. Prolonged or incorrect use may increase the risk of antimicrobial resistance, particularly for topical antibiotics (5, 13). Discussing the treatment regimen with patients (and/or parent/caregiver) reduces the risk that antibiotics will be incorrectly used (5). Where the patient (and/or parent/caregiver) ability and/or motivation to correctly use topical treatment is in doubt e.g., when there are multiple sores, oral antibiotics should be considered, or referral to an appropriate healthcare provider for IM benzathine benzylpenicillin (2, 5). Refer to the Primary Clinical Care Manual for further information (10).

gates.criterion: Patient is not at high risk of ARF and does not reside/recently reside in an endemic community (referral criteria do not apply - see PW-1-S4/PW-1-S5)
Infection is not widespread and multiple family/community members are not infected (otherwise topical antibiotics are not appropriate, due to the risk of rapid resistance)
If topical treatment is selected, the patient (and/or parent/caregiver) ability and motivation to correctly use topical treatment is not in doubt

steps.description: Confirm management is appropriate: Consult the Therapeutic Guidelines, Australian Medicines Handbook and other appropriate resources to confirm that management is appropriate, including for: contraindications and precautions; drug interactions; pregnancy and lactation. Reminder: The prescribing and use of antibiotics should be consistent with the principles described in the Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic. Pharmacists should carefully assess whether antibiotic therapy is clinically indicated, and if so, consider local antimicrobial resistance patterns and relevant clinical factors when selecting therapy.

gates.criterion: Management confirmed appropriate for contraindications and precautions, drug interactions, and pregnancy and lactation

steps.description: Communicate agreed management plan: Comprehensive advice and counselling (including supporting written information when required) should be provided to the patient regarding: individual product and medicine use; non-pharmacological measures; how to manage adverse effects; when to seek further care and/or treatment, including recognising complications of impetigo, particularly ARF and APSGN. It is the pharmacist's responsibility to ensure the suitability and accuracy of any resources provided to patients (and/or parents/caregivers) and to ensure compliance with all copyright conditions. The agreed management plan should be shared with members of the patient's multidisciplinary healthcare team, with the patient's consent. Patient resources: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Fact sheet: Impetigo (school sores) (20).

General measures for the patient, family and community to reduce the spread: 'The management of impetigo consists of pharmacotherapy in addition to general measures for the patient, family and community to reduce the spread (5).' 'Household contacts should be assessed and treated if affected.' Advice and education to reduce the spread of impetigo as per the Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic (Skin and soft tissue infections - Impetigo) (2) and the Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Impetigo (school sores) fact sheet (20) (page 6, Develop management plan).

General advice: At the time of initial consultation, patients (and/or parents/caregiver) should be advised to see an appropriate healthcare provider if: the condition does not improve within 5–10 days of starting treatment; the patient’s signs or symptoms worsen; the patient develops new signs or symptoms (e.g. systemic signs or symptoms); the condition reoccurs after treatment course is completed; the adverse effects of treatment cannot be managed in the pharmacy setting. (See RF-16 to RF-20.)

gates.criterion: None of the 'see an appropriate healthcare provider if' triggers present (RF-16 to RF-20)

steps.description: Clinical review: Clinical review is generally not required. Pharmacists should prescribe a quantity of medicine that aligns with the expected duration of therapy. Advise patients (and/or parents/caregivers) to see an appropriate healthcare provider if the condition does not improve or resolve (see Refer when and General advice).

gates.criterion: Condition improves or resolves (otherwise see 'Refer when' and 'General advice')

open_questions.topic: No printed exclusion criteria section - 'Refer when' bullets captured as exclusions
open_questions.observed: The document has no heading titled 'Exclusion criteria'. The fourteen bullets under 'Refer when' (page 2) are captured as EXC-1 to EXC-14 because the document directs referral rather than pharmacist treatment for those situations.
open_questions.why_unclear: Derivation from a referral heading rather than a printed eligibility exclusion list.

open_questions.topic: Combinatorics of the 'Refer when' list interpreted as any_of
open_questions.observed: Introductory wording is 'in the following situations:' followed by bullets with no explicit AND/OR statement; encoded as criteria_group.any_of (any one bullet triggers referral).
open_questions.why_unclear: Document does not state combinatorics for the bullet list; default interpretation recorded.

open_questions.topic: Specific topical and oral anti-infective agents, strengths, doses, frequencies and durations not printed
open_questions.observed: Pharmacotherapy is defined only as 'A topical or oral medicine mentioned in the Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic (Skin and soft tissue infections - Impetigo) (2)'. Route rules are printed (topical for nonrecurrent limited non-bullous impetigo up to 2 sores; oral for localised area with more than 2 sores), but no product names or dosing appear.
open_questions.why_unclear: Dose/strength/frequency are not in this document; no invented values were entered.

open_questions.topic: Gate outcome not stated - topical antibiotic route rule
open_questions.observed: 'Topical antibiotics are not appropriate if the infection is widespread or multiple family/community members are infected, due to the risk of rapid resistance (1-3).' The document does not state the single downstream action (switch to oral, refer, stop); on_fail recorded as 'unclear'. Note 'Refer when' separately requires referral when impetigo is widespread (RF-9).
open_questions.why_unclear: Restriction printed without a stated downstream action.

open_questions.topic: Gate outcome not stated - doubt about ability/motivation for topical treatment
open_questions.observed: 'Where the patient (and/or parent/caregiver) ability and/or motivation to correctly use topical treatment is in doubt e.g., when there are multiple sores, oral antibiotics should be considered, or referral to an appropriate healthcare provider for IM benzathine benzylpenicillin (2, 5).' Two alternative actions are printed ('should be considered, or referral'), so no single on_fail action could be chosen; recorded as 'unclear'.
open_questions.why_unclear: Branch with two permitted actions rather than one dictated action.

open_questions.topic: Gate outcome not stated - confirm management appropriate
open_questions.observed: PW-1-S7 gate 'management confirmed appropriate for contraindications and precautions, drug interactions, and pregnancy and lactation' has no stated failure action; on_fail recorded as 'unclear'.
open_questions.why_unclear: Document instructs confirmation but not the consequence of a failed check.

open_questions.observed: Page 3 prints 'Table 1. Types of impetigo (1, 2, 7, 11-13)' and page 5 prints 'Table 1. Individuals at high risk of developing ARF (2, 17, 19)'. The 'Refer when' bullets say '(refer to Table 1)' for both ARF high risk and endemic community - it is ambiguous which table is meant (the ARF risk table on page 5 is the only one containing residence/travel criteria).
open_questions.why_unclear: Duplicate table numbering in the source document.

open_questions.topic: Combinatorics of Table 1 ARF risk lists not stated
open_questions.observed: Table 1 lists four high-risk groups and then 'Additional risk factors for individuals aged ≤40 years (particularly between 5-20 years)' with two further bullets. The document does not state whether the additional factors combine with the main list by AND/OR, or whether 'resides, or has recently resided in an endemic community' maps to a specific bullet; gate outcomes recorded with high confidence for the referral direction but the exact predicate mapping is interpretive.
open_questions.why_unclear: No combinators printed for the risk tables.

open_questions.observed: 'patient resides, or has recently resided in an endemic community (refer to Table 1)' - the document does not define 'endemic community' or 'recently', and Table 1 refers to 'an area with a high rate of ARF e.g., refugees and migrants from low-middle income countries, rural and remote communities'.
open_questions.why_unclear: No numeric or place-list definition printed; structured form left null.

open_questions.observed: The document states 'Topical anti-infectives are considered sufficient treatment for patients with nonrecurrent limited non-bullous impetigo (up to 2 sores) who are not at high risk of ARF' and 'Pharmacists may prescribe oral antibiotics if impetigo is in a localised area with more than 2 sores'. TX-1 (topical anti-infectives) coded first_line=true on that 'considered sufficient' wording; TX-2 (oral antibiotics) coded first_line=false. The document does not use the words 'first line'.
open_questions.why_unclear: Line of therapy inferred from sufficiency wording, not an explicit ranking.

open_questions.observed: 'Refer the patient to an appropriate healthcare provider (including emergency services, if required)' is the only urgency wording printed; no trigger carries explicit 'urgent' language, so all referral triggers were coded severity 'medium' (not upgraded) and 'emergency services, if required' is recorded under referral.emergency.

'Service restricted to patients aged 1 year or over' sets a minimum of 1 year; no maximum age is stated (age_bounds.max_years = null). 'Impetigo commonly affects children between the ages of 2 and 5 but may also affect older children and adults (1)' is epidemiology, not an eligibility bound. Weight ('if a child') is collected in history but no weight-based dosing is printed.
open_questions.why_unclear: Document only states a lower bound.
